topic: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) and Smart Pointers
explanation: RAII is a fundamental C++ technique that ensures resources (like memory, files, network connections) are automatically managed.  It ties the lifetime of a resource to the lifetime of an object. When the object goes out of scope, its destructor is called, automatically releasing the resource. This prevents resource leaks and simplifies error handling. Smart pointers are crucial for implementing RAII for dynamically allocated objects.
syntax: Smart pointers, primarily `std::unique_ptr`, `std::shared_ptr`, and `std::weak_ptr`, are used to manage dynamically allocated objects.  `std::unique_ptr` provides exclusive ownership, `std::shared_ptr` allows shared ownership, and `std::weak_ptr` is used to observe a `shared_ptr` without increasing its reference count.  They are header-only;  `<memory>` must be included.
example_explanation: The example demonstrates how `std::unique_ptr` and `std::shared_ptr` manage the lifetime of a `Resource` object.  `unique_ptr` ensures the resource is released when it goes out of scope. `shared_ptr` handles multiple owners, releasing the resource only when the last owner goes out of scope.  This eliminates manual `delete` calls, a common source of memory leaks.  Using smart pointers is a best practice in modern C++, promoting safer and more maintainable code.  Failure to use smart pointers for dynamically allocated objects is a common pitfall, leading to memory leaks and dangling pointers.
